newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe bourse upbeat ahead of budget.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe bourse upbeat ahead of budget.

text.p: High liquidity and expectations of a positive national budget on Thursday should keep Zimbabwean stocks on a firm path this week, market analysts said on Monday.
Traditionally market players take to the sidelines ahead of the budget, but they have so far defied those trends, pushing the bourse to record highs every day for the past week.
The market's key industrial index soared four percent -- a record jump of 476.53 points -- last week to end Friday at 11,406.45, a new peak.
The market has been unfazed by recent wildcat strikes, higher annual inflation in June and speculation about an early El Nino phenomenon which might bring drought to southern Africa.
"It is clear that this upturn has been to a large extent liquidity driven with little regard to value or growth," said Sagit Stockbrokers research analyst Evan Green.
"With the budget coming through on Thursday, we don't expect the market to quieten down at all because there's a lot of liquidity in the market," he told Reuters.
The new budget will run for 18 months to December 1998 as the southern African country moves to a calendar year from the traditional July to June fiscal period.

"Traditionally the market is soft ahead of the budget but it is defying past trends and having a run before the budget and the main driving factor is liquidity," said Jason Moore of economic and market analysts Dataworld.
He and Green said the recent oversubscription by 10 times of national dairy Dairibord's public share offer indicated that there was money and appetite for equity investment.
"The extent of the oversubscription of the recent Dairibord offer surprised many and it is this excess liquidity which is driving the market higher," Green said.
"When will it end? With little in the way of attractive alternatives and a positive budget expected, heralding an extensive privatisation drive, there does not appear much to stop it," he said.
Following Dairibord's success, local economic analysts expect the government to finally roll out its long-awaited privatisation of loss-making state firms.
State firms to be privatised this year include the Cotton Company of Zimbabwe and the Commercial Bank of Zimbabwe, while the Zimbabwe Iron and Steel Company is slotted for offloading next year.

Green and other analysts say the sell-off of the state firms would help the government in its efforts to narrow its budget deficit, which has been widening off targets for the past seven years since Zimbabwe started implementing market-led economic reforms.
Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa a week ago pegged the government's spending deficit for the financial year ended June 30 at 10.3 percent of gross domestic product, off a target of 8.5 percent.
